The process by which a substance permeates into another — for example, a fluid soaking into a liquid or solid, or a substance passing through the skin into the body.
The gradual adjustment an organism makes to a new climate or environment, such as a change in altitude or temperature.
A small molecule central to carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism. It ferries an acetyl group into the citric acid cycle, where it is broken down to release energy.
Movement of molecules against a gradient using energy.
Describes an organism or process that requires the presence of oxygen to survive or occur.
An organic compound bearing both an amine and a carboxylic acid group. Chains of amino acids link together to build proteins.
Describes an organism or process that does not require molecular oxygen, and may even be poisoned by it.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
A member of the multicellular, eukaryotic kingdom Animalia. Most animals eat organic matter, breathe oxygen, move under their own power, and reproduce sexually.
A drug that kills or slows the growth of bacteria, used to treat or prevent bacterial infection.
Protein that identifies and neutralizes pathogens.
One of the three great domains of life, alongside Bacteria and Eukaryota — single-celled microbes that often thrive in extreme environments.
The deliberate breeding of plants or animals by humans to favor particular traits, as opposed to natural selection acting without human input.
Reproduction from a single parent that produces offspring genetically identical to that parent.
An organism able to make its own complex organic compounds from simple inorganic substances, usually by capturing energy from sunlight or chemical reactions. Contrast heterotroph.
A vast group of single-celled, prokaryotic microbes that lack a true nucleus, forming one of the three fundamental domains of life.
A virus that specifically infects and reproduces inside bacteria.
The way a single prokaryotic cell splits into two genetically identical daughter cells.
The two-part Latinized naming system used to formally classify every species, such as Homo sapiens.
The branch of science studying the chemical compounds, reactions, and processes occurring inside living organisms.
The total variety of life found across a habitat, ecosystem, or the entire planet.
The study of how species and ecosystems are distributed across geographic space and through geological time.
The use of computational tools to store, organize, and analyze large biological datasets such as genome sequences.
A large-scale ecological region, such as a desert or rainforest, defined by its climate and the plant and animal communities adapted to it.
The scientific study of plants, including their structure, growth, and classification.
The light-independent stage of photosynthesis, occurring in the chloroplast, in which carbon dioxide is converted into sugars using energy captured earlier as ATP and NADPH.
Uncontrolled cell division due to cycle malfunction.
Outer coating in bacteria for protection.
The conversion of inorganic carbon dioxide into organic compounds by living organisms, as happens in photosynthesis.
The basic structural and functional unit of every living organism — the smallest unit that can be considered alive on its own.
The ordered sequence of growth and division stages a cell passes through to duplicate its genetic material and split into daughter cells.
The thin, semipermeable barrier enclosing a cell's cytoplasm, controlling what enters and leaves.
Sum of all energy transformations in a cell.
Structure in plant cells that forms a new cell wall during division.
The foundational idea that all living things are composed of one or more cells.
A rigid outer layer found beyond the cell membrane in plants, fungi, and most prokaryotes, providing structural support.
Breakdown of glucose to produce energy.
The principle describing how genetic information generally flows within a cell — often summarized as 'DNA makes RNA, and RNA makes protein.'
Region where sister chromatids are joined.
Control point in the cell cycle to ensure accuracy.
The green pigment in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria that captures light energy to drive photosynthesis.
The specialized organelle in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis takes place.
DNA-protein complex that condenses into chromosomes.
A tightly coiled strand of DNA found in the cell nucleus that carries an organism's genes in linear order.
Also called the Krebs cycle — a chain of reactions that oxidizes nutrient-derived molecules to release usable chemical energy in nearly all aerobic organisms.
Indentation in animal cells during cytokinesis.
The theory explaining how immune cells multiply in response to a specific invading antigen, forming the basis of the adaptive immune response.
The study of Earth's biodiversity aimed at protecting species, habitats, and ecosystems from extinction and degradation.
The independent evolution of similar traits in unrelated species, often because they face similar environmental pressures.
Exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes.
Protein that regulates the cell cycle.
Enzyme activated by cyclin for cycle control.
Division of the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
Everything inside a cell's membrane except the nucleus — a gel-like fluid holding the organelles and dissolved molecules.
A dynamic internal scaffold of protein filaments that gives a cell its shape and enables movement and internal transport.
A measure of an organism's genetic contribution to the next generation, typically judged by how many offspring survive to reproduce.
An organism, such as many fungi and bacteria, that breaks down dead organic material and recycles its nutrients back into the ecosystem.
The unfolding or structural collapse of a protein or nucleic acid, often triggered by heat, extreme pH, or harsh chemicals.
The double-stranded molecule that stores hereditary information in nearly all living organisms, built from four repeating chemical letters: A, C, G, and T.
The study of how organisms grow, develop, and change from a single fertilized cell into a mature form.
Movement of molecules from high to low concentration.
Enzyme that adds nucleotides to replicate DNA.
Process of making an identical copy of DNA.
The scientific study of how organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment.
A community of living organisms interacting with the non-living parts of their environment as a single functioning system.
An organism, often called 'cold-blooded,' whose body temperature is largely set by its surrounding environment rather than internal heat production. Contrast endotherm.
A series of protein complexes in the mitochondria that pass electrons along a chain to power the production of ATP, the cell's main energy currency.
The early developmental stage of a multicellular organism, beginning shortly after fertilization.
A species at serious risk of extinction, often due to habitat loss, hunting, disease, or climate change.
The condition of a species being found naturally in only one specific geographic area and nowhere else.
The network of glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate growth, metabolism, and other body functions.
Process of taking materials into the cell.
Network for protein and lipid synthesis.
The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as free-living prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell, eventually becoming permanent internal partners.
An organism, often called 'warm-blooded,' that generates and regulates its own internal body heat regardless of the surrounding temperature. Contrast ectotherm.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions inside cells without itself being consumed, making metabolism fast enough to sustain life.
The study of how diseases spread through populations, including their causes, patterns, and prevention.
The study of heritable changes in how genes are expressed that occur without any change to the underlying DNA sequence itself.
An organism whose cells contain a true, membrane-bound nucleus — includes all animals, plants, fungi, and protists. Contrast prokaryote.
The change in heritable traits of a population across successive generations, driven by mechanisms such as mutation, gene flow, natural selection, and genetic drift.
The process by which a cell expels molecules to its exterior by fusing a membrane-bound sac with the cell membrane.
The permanent disappearance of an entire species or other group of organisms, marked by the death of its last surviving individual.
A metabolic process that breaks down sugar for energy without requiring oxygen.
A conceptual map relating genetic variation to reproductive success, used to visualize how populations evolve toward more favorable traits over time.
The loss of genetic diversity that occurs when a new population is established by only a small number of founding individuals.
Eukaryotic kingdom with chitin cell walls.
Resting phase where cells stop dividing.
Part of interphase where the cell grows and performs normal functions.
Final phase of interphase; cell prepares for mitosis.
A reproductive cell — such as a sperm or egg — that carries half the genetic material needed to form a new offspring when it fuses with another gamete.
A segment of DNA that carries the instructions to build a specific RNA or protein product, and the basic hereditary unit passed from parent to offspring.
Conversion of DNA information into traits.
The complete collection of genes and their variants present within a population or species.
Random chance-driven changes in how common a particular gene variant is within a population, unrelated to whether that variant is helpful or harmful.
The scientific study of heredity and how traits are passed from one generation to the next.
The complete set of genetic material contained within an organism's cells.
The specific genetic makeup of an organism that underlies and helps determine its observable traits, or phenotype.
The natural physical environment in which a particular organism typically lives and thrives.
Enzyme that unwinds the DNA strand.
The passing of traits from parents to offspring, occurring through either sexual or asexual reproduction.
An organism that cannot make its own food and must consume other organisms or organic matter for energy. Contrast autotroph.
An organism's ability to maintain a stable internal environment — such as temperature or pH — despite changes in outside conditions.
Pair of chromosomes with the same genes.
A signaling molecule, produced by a gland, that travels through the bloodstream to regulate the activity of distant organs and tissues.
Random distribution of chromosomes in meiosis.
Longest phase of the cell cycle where the cell grows and replicates DNA.
An animal that lacks a backbone, a category that includes insects, mollusks, and worms among many others. Contrast vertebrate.
Protein allowing ions to pass through membranes.
Protein complex where spindle fibers attach.
A distinct juvenile stage that many animals — such as insects and amphibians — pass through before metamorphosing into their adult form.
The full sequence of developmental stages an organism passes through, from formation to reproduction and eventually to the birth of the next generation.
Large-scale evolutionary change occurring at or above the level of species, in contrast with the smaller, generation-to-generation shifts studied in microevolution.
A specialized form of cell division that halves the chromosome number to produce genetically unique reproductive cells, such as eggs and sperm.
Movement of substances across the cell membrane.
The full set of chemical reactions within an organism that convert food into energy and building blocks for growth, repair, and function.
A dramatic physical transformation an organism undergoes during development, such as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
Chromosomes line up at the cell's equatorial plane.
Spread of cancer cells to other body parts.
The branch of biology devoted to studying microscopic organisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa.
The organelle often called the cell's 'powerhouse,' where aerobic respiration generates most of a cell's usable energy.
The stage of the cell cycle in which a cell's duplicated chromosomes separate into two identical nuclei, ultimately producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
Period of cell division that includes mitosis and cytokinesis.
The branch of biology concerned with the molecular basis of biological activity, particularly the structure and function of DNA, RNA, and proteins.
Made up of many cells working together.
A change in a DNA sequence, which can arise spontaneously or from exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, and can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial.
The scientific study of fungi, including their genetics, classification, and uses.
The process by which organisms with traits better suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more successfully, passing those traits on more often.
A specialized, electrically excitable cell that receives, processes, and transmits information via electrical and chemical signals.
The specific role and set of resource needs an organism occupies within its ecosystem, including how it feeds, shelters, and reproduces.
The natural process, largely carried out by specialized microorganisms, that converts atmospheric nitrogen gas into forms usable by living organisms.
Membrane around the nucleus that breaks during prophase.
A large biomolecule — DNA or RNA — built from repeating nucleotide units, essential for storing and transmitting genetic information.
The membrane-bound structure in eukaryotic cells that houses the cell's genetic material and directs its activities.
Structure composed of tissues working together.
A specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function, such as the mitochondria or chloroplast.
Any individual living thing, capable of carrying out the processes associated with life.
The passive movement of water across a semipermeable membrane, from an area of lower solute concentration to one of higher concentration.
The scientific study of ancient life through the examination of fossils preserved in Earth's crust.
An organism that lives on or inside a host organism, drawing nutrients from it, typically to the host's detriment.
Any agent, such as a virus, bacterium, or fungus, capable of causing disease in a host organism.
Breaks down fatty acids and detoxifies.
Type of endocytosis where the cell engulfs solid particles.
The observable physical, biochemical, or behavioral traits of an organism, produced by the interaction of its genotype with the environment.
The process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy, producing sugars from carbon dioxide and water while releasing oxygen.
The evolutionary history and relatedness of a group of organisms, often represented as a branching tree diagram.
The branch of biology studying how living organisms and their parts function, including all their physical and chemical processes.
Hair-like structures on bacteria for attachment.
Regulates what enters and exits the cell.
The transfer of pollen from the male to the female part of a flower, a necessary step toward plant fertilization and seed production.
A group of organisms of the same species living in the same geographic area and capable of interbreeding with one another.
An interaction in which one organism, the predator, hunts and consumes another, the prey.
An organism, such as a bacterium, whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Contrast eukaryote.
Chromosomes condense and spindle fibers begin to form.
A large molecule built from chains of amino acids, serving as a structural component, enzyme, signaling molecule, or transporter within a cell.
Detects and responds to chemical signals.
Process of breaking down glucose for energy.
A nucleic acid that carries out several roles in gene expression, including copying genetic instructions from DNA and helping build proteins.
DNA replication phase of the cell cycle.
Ability of the membrane to choose what enters/exits.
Process of converting signals into cellular responses.

A group of organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring, generally treated as the basic unit of biological classification.
Protein structures that move chromosomes during mitosis.
Undifferentiated cell that can develop into specialized cells.
Molecule on which an enzyme acts.
A close, long-term biological interaction between two different species, which may benefit both, benefit one while harming the other, or benefit one without affecting the other.
Pairing of homologous chromosomes in meiosis.
The scientific practice of naming, describing, and classifying organisms into a structured hierarchy of groups.
Group of four chromatids formed during meiosis.
Group of similar cells performing a function.
Process of copying DNA into mRNA.
mRNA is decoded to create proteins.
An organism's position in a food chain, such as producer, primary consumer, or top predator, reflecting how energy flows through an ecosystem.
Prepares the immune system to fight pathogens.
Storage organelle for water and nutrients.
An animal possessing a backbone, a group that includes fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Contrast invertebrate.
A microscopic infectious agent that can only replicate inside the living cells of a host organism, existing at the boundary between living and non-living matter.
The branch of biology devoted to the study of animals, their behavior, physiology, and classification.
